hints: With [2,1,2], swapping the two 2s gives the same ordering. When picking a value for a position, does it matter which copy of 2 you take?

Sort nums and backtrack with used[]. Skip nums[i] when it equals nums[i-1] and nums[i-1] is not used: this forces equal copies to be placed in left-to-right order, so each distinct ordering is built once.

1. Sort nums; create used[].
  2. If cur is full, save a copy.
  3. Loop i: skip if used[i].
  4. Also skip if i > 0, nums[i] == nums[i-1] and !used[i-1].
  5. Choose, recurse, un-choose.

approaches.name: Brute force + set
approaches.idea: Generate all n! orderings and keep the unique ones in a set.

approaches.name: Optimal: sorted backtracking with duplicate rule
approaches.idea: Never build a repeated ordering, so the work is proportional to the number of distinct orderings.

explain: Sorted, [2,1,2] becomes [1,2,2]. Putting 1 first gives 1,2,2. Putting the first 2 first gives 2,1,2 and 2,2,1. Trying the second 2 first is skipped because the first 2 is equal and unused. So exactly 3 orderings come out. The rule keeps a fixed order among equal copies; for [0,0] only one ordering survives.
recognize: 'Every distinct ordering' + 'may contain duplicates' → sort, then permutation backtracking that skips an equal value whose left twin is unused.
